---
title: "Advanced Mathematics for Competitive Programming"
subtitle: "A textbook for expert programmers building mathematical foundations"
---

You already know how to write a fast segment tree, how to squeeze a flow
algorithm under the time limit, and how to debug a tricky DP at two in the
morning. Then a problem says *count the labelled forests modulo $998244353$*,
or *find $x$ with $x^2 \equiv a \pmod p$*, and the difficulty is no longer
engineering. The obstacle is a piece of mathematics that editorials name in
one line and never explain.

This book is the missing explanation. It develops the algebra, number theory,
counting, and probability behind hard ICPC, Codeforces, and AtCoder problems,
starting from definitions and assuming no university mathematics — only that
you are a confident programmer who can follow a careful argument.

Start with [mathematical foundations](00-foundations/chapter.qmd),
then follow the [learning path](STUDY_PLAN.qmd). Keep the
[notation and algebra contracts](NOTATION.qmd) open as a reference.

## What a chapter looks like

Every chapter follows the same rhythm, because that is the order in which
ideas actually become usable:

1. **A problem you cannot yet solve.** Concrete, contest-shaped, and
   deliberately just out of reach.
2. **The object that solves it**, introduced in plain words before any
   notation, with a small example you can check by hand.
3. **Why the central formula is true.** Not a citation — a derivation you
   could reproduce on paper during a contest.
4. **The algorithm's contract:** what it assumes, what it returns, what it
   costs, and the inputs on which it silently returns garbage.
5. **Practice**, from recognizing the model to combining several of them.

The failure modes are not an appendix. Knowing that Fermat inversion breaks
the moment the modulus is composite, or that a formula needs $n < p$ because
it divides by a factorial, is exactly the knowledge that separates a correct
submission from a wrong-answer verdict you cannot explain.

## How to study

Read the derivations with a pen. When a chapter says *why this is true*,
close the page and try to rebuild the argument; the gap you find is the part
you did not actually understand. Work the small numerical examples by hand —
they are chosen so that a misconception produces a visibly wrong number.

Attempt the original exercises before opening their solutions. Use the
external contest problems to practice modelling under uncertainty. Difficulty
labels are relative to this course; they are not predicted contest ratings.
Some exercise pages deliberately point forward to applications that need a
later chapter, and identify those extra prerequisites.

The book assumes you already have a tested competitive-programming library,
so it contains almost no code. It teaches mathematical models, correctness
invariants, input/output contracts, and resource bounds; the implementations
stay in your library. No routine should be selected merely because its name
resembles a phrase in the problem statement.

## Curriculum at a glance {#dependency-map}

Read foundations first, then use these branches. Arrows show the main conceptual
dependencies; the [learning path](STUDY_PLAN.qmd) gives chapter-level details.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  F["Proofs and notation"] --> A["Modular algebra"]
  F --> C["Counting"]
  A --> B["Binomials modulo anything"]
  C --> B
  A --> N["Divisor sums and sieves"]
  A --> L["Linear algebra and recurrences"]
  A --> P["Polynomials and formal series"]
  C --> G["Symmetry and generating functions"]
  P --> G
  C --> T["Subset transforms and set series"]
  L --> R["Probability systems and algebraic graphs"]
  G --> H["Holonomic methods"]
  B --> Q["q-Analogues and subspaces"]
  L --> Q
  N --> X["Mixed and frontier capstones"]
  Q --> X
  R --> X
  T --> X
  H --> X
```

Chapter numbers are the reading order: chapter $n$ relies only on earlier
chapters. Detours are still allowed — the [learning path](STUDY_PLAN.qmd)
lists, for each chapter, the few earlier ones it genuinely uses.

## Chapters

### I · Arithmetic and counting

- [00 · Mathematical foundations and proof](00-foundations/chapter.qmd): notation, logic, induction, invariants, extremal arguments, Bézout, double counting.
- [01 · Modular algebra](01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd): units, fields, CRT, orders, valuations, logarithms, modular roots.
- [02 · Multiplicative number theory](02-multiplicative-number-theory/chapter.qmd): factorization, arithmetic functions, gcd filters, divisor inversion, Gaussian integers.
- [03 · Combinatorics](03-combinatorics/chapter.qmd) and [practice](03-combinatorics/exercises.qmd): inclusion–exclusion, Stirling and Catalan models, partitions, binomial transforms, rook polynomials.
- [04 · Binomial coefficients modulo anything](04-modular-binomials/chapter.qmd): Lucas, Kummer carries, prime-power factorials, composite moduli by CRT.
- [05 · Group actions](05-group-actions/chapter.qmd) and [practice](05-group-actions/exercises.qmd): orbits, stabilizers, Burnside, Pólya, induced graph symmetries.

### II · Algebraic engines

- [06 · Polynomials](06-polynomials/chapter.qmd) and [practice](06-polynomials/exercises.qmd): convolution, Fourier evaluation, division, product trees, interpolation, Taylor shift.
- [07 · Linear algebra](07-linear-algebra/chapter.qmd): vector spaces, rank, determinants, XOR bases, tree counts, recurrences and black-box methods.
- [08 · Transforms](08-transforms/chapter.qmd): subset and divisor inversion, OR/AND/XOR, ranked disjoint convolution.
- [09 · Formal power series](09-formal-power-series/chapter.qmd) and [practice](09-formal-power-series/exercises.qmd): precision, Newton lifting, inverse, logarithm, exponential, composition and reversion.
- [10 · Generating functions](10-generating-functions/chapter.qmd) and [practice](10-generating-functions/exercises.qmd): labelled and unlabelled models, rational sequences, coefficient extraction, Lagrange inversion.
- [11 · Set power series](11-set-power-series/chapter.qmd): disjoint multiplication, connected components, set exponential and logarithm.

### III · Models and synthesis

- [12 · Probability](12-probability/chapter.qmd): sample spaces, indicators, conditioning, variance, stochastic DP and absorbing systems.
- [13 · Discrete sums and Diophantine tools](13-discrete-sums/chapter.qmd): interpolation, differences, floor sums, rational approximation, Pell equations.
- [14 · Summatory sieves](14-advanced-sieves/chapter.qmd): quotient states, prefix recurrences, prime sums, multiplicative enumeration, powerful support.
- [15 · Mixed capstones](15-capstones/chapter.qmd): modelling workshops with complete reduction guidance.

### IV · Frontier topics

- [16 · q-Analogues and subspace counting](16-q-analogues/chapter.qmd): Gaussian binomials, division-free recurrences, rank distributions.
- [17 · Finite-field polynomials](17-finite-field-polynomials/chapter.qmd): quotient fields, Frobenius, factorization and irreducibility certification.
- [18 · Algebraic graph methods](18-algebraic-graph-methods/chapter.qmd): polynomial identity testing, Pfaffians, Tutte matrices, weighted matching.
- [19 · Holonomic methods](19-holonomic-methods/chapter.qmd): differential equations, polynomial-coefficient recurrences, guessing and certification.
- [20 · Frontier capstones](20-frontier-capstones/chapter.qmd): synthesis with explicit hypotheses, small models and validation plans.

## What mastery means

For each chapter, record whether you can define its objects, reproduce its
central proof, solve its local exercises, recognize its model in a contest
statement, and explain a counterexample to its misuse. Revisit a difficult
problem after two and six weeks; successful recall of the derivation is more
informative than recognizing an editorial.

The course concentrates on algebra, number theory, counting, and probability.
Geometry and continuous optimization are outside this curriculum. No finite
toolkit covers every future contest problem; the transferable skill is deriving
a new variant from well-understood objects and assumptions.

See the [source and verification policy](SOURCES.qmd) for reference standards.
